Chapter One: How Stories Shape What People Think About Indigenous Peoples
Ever notice how so much of what we think we know about Indigenous communities doesn’t come from real-life encounters, but from stories? Stories we hear in classrooms, see in movies, or pick up in quiet family chats. Over time, these stories get repeated so often, they become the lens most people use to see Native folks—even when those stories have more fiction than truth.
Picture a kid, sitting in a schoolroom, listening to a teacher talk about the so-called “discovery” of a continent. The lesson sounds neat and simple—explorers arrive, they find empty land, and that’s where history apparently begins. Maybe that kid draws a ship, or a feathered headdress, not realizing the real story is way messier, full of voices and experiences that get left out. Most of us grow up with these stories, rarely asking why the “Indian” is just a side character, or why our own ancestors always get to be the heroes.
Now, think about family movie nights across North America—old Westerns flickering on TV. The “Indian” on screen is always one of two things: a noble warrior, or a faceless threat. You never see them with a job, a family, or a sense of humor. We laugh or gasp with the story, but hardly ever pause to wonder what life’s really like for the people being shown. Over the years, these images settle in, shaping how we react when we actually meet a Native person—if that ever happens.
The stories that stick are the ones that make things simple. There’s the “dead Indian”—a figure from the past, frozen in time, who doesn’t ask for anything. Then there’s the “noble Indian”—wise and tragic, here to teach us a lesson or die bravely. And finally, there’s the “live Indian”—the one who’s inconvenient, still here, still asking questions, still wanting land and rights. Most folks would rather stick with the first two.
Here’s something to pay attention to—these stories aren’t just harmless entertainment. They shape who gets to be heard, who gets believed, and who gets ignored. When you hear a government official talk about “helping” Native communities, those words are colored by the same old stories. When a neighbor complains about “special treatment” for Indigenous people, that complaint is rooted in myth, not fact.
Most people don’t even notice how these stories are designed to keep things comfortable for those in power. They gloss over the hard parts—broken treaties, stolen land, families torn apart. They turn real people into symbols, so nobody has to feel guilty or responsible. The end result? Indigenous voices are always in the background, rarely at the center.
But every so often, someone interrupts the story. Maybe a parent at a school meeting asks why the curriculum skips over residential schools. Or a young person wonders why their favorite movie never shows Native people as anything but obstacles. These moments might seem small, but they matter. They remind us—the story isn’t over. The people being talked about? They’re still here, still watching, and still telling their own stories.
